narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 65.9% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction as a key factor, your law school application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three pieces of information about you, ranked by importance. Your LSAT score was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward failure. At 34, it sits noticeably below the average of 37.2 among students who were accepted, and this gap significantly increased the model’s concern about your likelihood of passing the bar.

Next, your first-year law school grades (decile ranking of 6) also pulled the prediction toward failure. Although this matches the average for accepted students, the model still saw it as contributing to higher risk in this specific combination of factors.

Your family income bracket of Middle was the third most influential factor and, like the others, nudged the outcome toward failure rather than success. While middle-income students make up about 35% of accepted applicants, the model interpreted this background, together with the other details, as part of a pattern associated with higher bar failure rates.

Taken together, these elements led the system to conclude your risk of not passing the bar was too high for admission. To improve your chances in the future, focus on raising your LSAT score through targeted preparation, as this was the single biggest driver. Strengthening your academic performance in law school and seeking additional bar exam support resources could also help demonstrate stronger readiness next time.
